caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No — and the man who made it wanted you to find out.

On October 16, 1869, two men hired to dig a well behind William "Stub" Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, struck a ten-foot stone man. Newell put a tent over it and charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute look. Three to five hundred people came a day. Cardiff's hotels and restaurants saw more custom in four days than ever before.

The giant was carved from a gypsum block quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, by George Hull, a tobacconist who had lost an argument with a Methodist preacher about the giants in Genesis 6:4. The quarrymen were told the stone was for a Lincoln monument. In Chicago, sculptors Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann shaped it to Hull's own body. Hull learned from a geologist that hair does not petrify, so the giant has none. Its skin was beaten with steel knitting needles to fake pores, then washed in sulphuric acid.

Geologist John F. Boynton said it was no fossil, but guessed a 17th-century Jesuit carved it. Cornell's Andrew D. White noticed there was no reason to dig a well there at all — the spot was convenient to neither house nor barn. Yale's Othniel C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug": soluble gypsum buried for centuries would not keep fresh tool marks.

Hull confessed on December 10, 1869. He said he did it proudly, to show how easily people believe.

What is not settled: whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter, knew what he was making. And the copy in a Michigan arcade is only claimed to be Barnum's.

Images: an 1869 lithograph of "The Onondaga Giant" (Popular Graphic Arts); a 1910 Bain News Service negative; and an 1873 stereograph of Cardiff Glen, Iowa, from the New York Public Library.
